name: What to pay for?
purpose: Why do two computer programmers earn €40,820 and €52,890? Pay decisions rest on three groups of reasons (≈ 20 reasons).

parts.label: Internal consistency
points: Valuing jobs relative to one another
Complexity, danger, unsocial hours, shift work
Part of core business, source of competitive advantage

parts.label: External competitiveness
points: Pay's role in quits and recruitment

parts.label: Individual characteristics
points: Unwise or illegal allocation of rewards (gender, age, ethnicity, looks)

apply: Sort every pay difference in the case into one of the three groups
Flag differences that only come from individual characteristics – unwise or illegal (EU pay transparency!)
Recommend what the firm should pay for, given its strategy
example: Chris (€40,820) vs Pat (€52,890): Pat's job requires more languages, beta testing and QC, a Master's and 4 years' experience (internal); Pat's firm is larger, more profitable, unionized, in the computer industry with few applicants (external).

name: Pat vs Chris: the reasons in detail
purpose: Which concrete reasons belong to internal consistency and which to external competitiveness?
apply: Quote the case facts next to each reason – that is the analysis the exam rewards
pitfalls: Putting “experience” under external – it is a property of the job requirements (internal)

name: From job analysis to salary structure
purpose: How do internal consistency and external competitiveness combine into a pay structure?

parts.label: Internal consistency
points: Job evaluation: value of jobs relative to each other

apply: Explain a pay problem as a missing step: no job analysis, no job evaluation, or no market benchmark

name: Individual contributions: pay for skills vs pay for performance
purpose: Should we reward what people can do or what they achieve?
apply: Choose by the job: skills pay where outputs are hard to measure or learning matters; performance pay where output is measurable and controllable

name: Why might PRP work?
purpose: Four mechanisms through which performance-related pay can raise performance.

parts.label: Culture
points: Signals what the firm values: a performance culture

parts.label: Keep the good
points: Sorting: attracts and retains high performers, low performers leave

parts.label: Focused effort
points: Agency theory: directs effort to the principal's goals

apply: For each mechanism, check whether the case conditions allow it to work
pitfalls: Forgetting sorting – at Safelite part of the gain came from who joined and stayed

name: Vroom's expectancy theory
purpose: When does a reward motivate effort? Only if all three links hold.

parts.label: Expectancy
points: “If I try harder I will do better”

parts.label: Instrumentality
points: “If I do better I will be rewarded”

apply: Test each link with case facts – one weak link breaks motivation
Expectancy breaks if results depend on rivals, markets or the boss
Instrumentality breaks if bonus criteria are unclear or discretionary
Valence breaks if the sum is small or the reward is not wanted
pitfalls: Collective PRP weakens line of sight: effort → performance → MY reward gets weaker
example: National Office Supplies: no written criteria + manager discretion → weak instrumentality.

name: Agency theory
purpose: How does the principal (firm) make the agent (worker) act in the principal's interest – and not shirk?

parts.label: Supervision
points: Costly when work is hard to observe

apply: Ask: is behaviour observable (→ supervise) or only output (→ incentives)?
Check the risk of rewarding the measurable part only (multitasking problem)
pitfalls: Incentives tied to the wrong output – the financial sector rewarded short-term results without risk

name: Effect of PRP on performance: the debate
origin: Lazear (2000) · Fernie & Metcalf (1999) · Marsden et al. (2009)
purpose: What does the evidence say – does PRP raise performance?

parts.label: Examples of success
points: Safelite (Lazear, 2000): piece rates for windscreen installers – output up sharply, pay up, labour cost per unit down
Jockeys (Fernie & Metcalf, 1999): performance pay → better results

parts.label: But… (Marsden et al., 2009)
points: Only 33 % agree PRP recognises good work
51.5 % say PRP is a good principle
36 % say it made them aware of objectives
Only 17 % say it gave incentives to work beyond requirements

apply: Use Safelite to show the conditions where PRP works, Marsden to show why it often fails in practice

name: Practical problems with PRP
origin: Session 6 · video on challenges to the use of rewards
purpose: Why is PRP hard to make work in practice?

parts.label: Identification & measurement
points: What is performance, and can it be measured?

parts.label: Need for precision
points: Small rating errors → big pay differences

parts.label: Contingency & contiguity
points: Contingency: reward clearly depends on performance
Contiguity: reward follows performance closely in time

apply: Run the case scheme through the five problems; each one you find is a design fix to recommend
pitfalls: PRP schemes are totally dependent on performance management systems
example: Vatican: “dedication, professionalism, productivity and politeness” – measurement problems and cultural clash. City bonuses: losses appear years later → clash with contiguity.

name: When does PRP work? Conditions from the cases
origin: Synthesis of the PRP case studies (Safelite, City banks, Vatican)
purpose: A test to decide whether – and how strongly – to use PRP in a case.

parts.label: Measure matches the real goal
points: Safelite yes · City no (no risk adjustment) · Vatican mostly subjective

parts.label: Employee controls the result
points: Safelite yes · City partly (markets) · Vatican few units

parts.label: Results known before payment
points: Safelite yes · City no (losses come later)

parts.label: Employee bears cost of failure
points: Safelite: unpaid rework · City: bonus kept

parts.label: Fits motivation & culture
points: Vatican: risk of crowding out mission-driven motivation

apply: Score the case on the five conditions
Match incentive strength to measure quality; match payment horizon to when results are known (defer with clawback)
Measure quantity and quality together; protect a pay floor
example: Safelite: guaranteed hourly floor + unpaid rework kept quality; output and pay both rose. Stiglitz: bankers were paid to gamble – share of gains, not of losses; hold bonuses in escrow.
